evals.expected_output: Several things on the site push assistants toward v1. (1) The v3 page as served is an empty JavaScript shell (generic title 'Quillpay Docs', empty #root, content fetched from JSON at runtime). Google can render JS, but Google itself notes not all bots run JavaScript, so many AI crawlers and fetchers likely see no v3 content at all. Server-render or pre-render the v3 docs, with a real title and description. (2) The sitemap lists only v1 and v2, leaves out v3, and stamps every URL with the same nightly lastmod. Google only uses lastmod when it's consistently accurate, and it ignores changefreq/priority. Add the v3 URLs and emit real modification dates. (3) The v1 page has no deprecation notice and a self-canonical, and its title/description read like the current way to take payments. Keep v1 live and indexable for existing customers, but add a prominent visible deprecation banner with the shutoff date and a link to the v3 equivalent. Put 'v1 (deprecated)' in titles and make the v3 page the one linked from navigation and the docs home. Canonicalizing v1 to v3 is only appropriate where the pages are true equivalents, and it's a strong signal, not a command. Don't block v1 in robots.txt or noindex it as a way of 'choosing' v3: robots.txt isn't a canonicalization tool and noindex removes the page entirely. Also publish a migration guide (v1 to v3 mapping) as plain HTML, and update code samples, SDK READMEs, and Q&A answers you control. Set expectations too: answers grounded in live retrieval can change as pages are recrawled, but what a model learned in training about v1 lags and won't change until future model updates. Then re-test the same prompts over time.

assertions.text: Identifies from the fixture that the v3 page's content is not present in the served HTML (an empty app shell with a generic title, filled in by JavaScript at runtime), and explains that crawlers or fetchers that don't execute JavaScript would see no v3 content.
assertions.rationale: Google's JS SEO basics say not all bots can run JavaScript and recommend server-side or pre-rendering; the fixture shows an empty #root.

assertions.text: Notes that the sitemap omits the v3 URLs and/or that its identical, auto-generated lastmod dates are unreliable; does not claim that changefreq or priority values will help Google (Google ignores them).
assertions.rationale: Google uses lastmod only if it is consistently and verifiably accurate and ignores priority and changefreq.

assertions.text: Does not recommend blocking the v1 docs in robots.txt as the way to make v3 the preferred version, and does not present noindex as a canonicalization tool; if it suggests noindexing v1 at all, it acknowledges that noindex removes those pages from search entirely (including for existing v1 users). If canonicalization is discussed, rel=canonical is treated as a strong signal rather than a guaranteed outcome and is limited to pages that are genuinely duplicate or very similar.
assertions.rationale: Google: 'Don't use the robots.txt file for canonicalization purposes'; 'We don't recommend using noindex to prevent selection of a canonical page within a single site' (noindex blocks the page from Search entirely); rel=canonical is 'a strong signal'; Google decides which pages are duplicates 'based on similarity of content'.

assertions.text: Recommends keeping v1 docs accessible but clearly marked as deprecated on the page itself (e.g., a visible notice with the shutoff date and a link to the v3 equivalent or a migration guide).
assertions.rationale: The user can't remove v1; on-page deprecation context is what any retrieving engine or reader will see alongside the v1 code.

assertions.text: Distinguishes between answers based on live retrieval/search (which can change as pages are recrawled) and what a model learned in training (which lags until future model updates), and sets expectations accordingly.
assertions.rationale: Stale API code in AI answers often comes from training data, so site fixes alone won't immediately change every answer.

assertions.text: Suggests verifying progress by re-running representative developer questions across the named assistants over time, rather than treating one check as conclusive.
assertions.rationale: AI answers vary between runs and engines, so before/after comparison needs repeated sampling.

evals.topic: Healthcare/YMYL: E-E-A-T and medical accuracy on a clinic's condition page
evals.prompt: I own Harbor Line Physical Therapy in Portland (three PTs). Our sciatica page used to bring in a lot of patients, but now Google's AI Overviews and ChatGPT answer sciatica questions by citing hospitals and the NHS, never us. My web agency says we need more 'E-E-A-T signals' and suggested adding a doctor reviewer to the schema, which I did. Page and my notes are attached. What should I do so AI answers cite us?
evals.expected_output: The page has bigger problems than missing signals, and some of them could hurt patients. Fix those first. Medically: it promises a 7-day permanent cure and '100% pain-free', but that figure comes from the 14 self-selected responders who finished the program. It tells readers to stop prescribed medication and says they never need a referral or imaging. That's unsafe. Authoritative sources say most sciatica improves over weeks to months, and certain symptoms (sciatica on both sides, severe or worsening weakness or numbness in both legs, numbness around the genitals or anus, bladder/bowel changes) need emergency care. Under the FTC's health-claims guidance, a cure/efficacy claim like this needs competent and reliable scientific evidence, generally RCTs, which the clinic doesn't have. Structured data: the reviewedBy neurosurgeon has never read the page and isn't named on it, lastReviewed is false (the footer says 2019), and the aggregateRating is the clinic's own GBP reviews copied in. That's markup that doesn't reflect visible content, a self-serving review, and a misrepresentation. Remove it. On E-E-A-T: Google says it isn't a specific ranking factor, though for YMYL topics its systems give more weight to content showing strong E-E-A-T. You can't add it with schema. Rewrite the page with the clinic's real expertise. Use bylines from the licensed DPTs (including the OCS), with credentials and a real review date. Give accurate, guideline-consistent information and cite reputable sources. Add red-flag guidance on when to seek urgent care. Describe what PT can realistically do, and what the clinic's own outcome data shows, with honest methodology. For a local clinic, AI answers to general medical questions will often still cite hospitals and national bodies. Your realistic wins are local/intent queries ('physical therapy for sciatica in Portland') and being an accurate, trustworthy source. No change can guarantee a citation.

assertions.text: Flags as potentially harmful the page's advice to stop prescribed medication and/or its claim that no referral or imaging is ever needed, and recommends removing or correcting it.
assertions.rationale: On a YMYL health page, advice that could lead readers to stop treatment or miss serious pathology is a patient-safety issue first, and a visibility issue second.

assertions.text: Identifies that the '7-day cure' / '100% pain-free' claims are unsupported (e.g., based on 14 self-selected responders) and/or inconsistent with mainstream medical information (e.g., sciatica usually gets better over a few weeks to a few months; some symptoms need emergency care).
assertions.rationale: NHS: 'Sciatica usually gets better in a few weeks to a few months'; sciatica on both sides, severe or worsening weakness or numbness in both legs, numbness around the genitals or anus, or new bladder/bowel problems need emergency care. The owner's notes give the 14-patient basis.

assertions.text: If it discusses the legal or regulatory exposure of the cure/efficacy claims, it does so accurately and without inventing specific rules or penalties (e.g., US FTC guidance holds health claims to a 'competent and reliable scientific evidence' standard, generally meaning randomized controlled human trials for health benefit claims).
assertions.rationale: The FTC Health Products Compliance Guidance (2022) sets the 'competent and reliable scientific evidence' standard and calls RCTs the most reliable evidence, generally expected for health benefit claims. It is written for health products, not services, so an answer that removes the false claims on safety and honesty grounds without a legal discussion is also correct.

assertions.text: Recommends removing or correcting the structured data that misrepresents the page: the reviewedBy physician who never reviewed it and isn't shown on the page, and/or the false lastReviewed date, and/or the copied-in aggregateRating.
assertions.rationale: Google: 'Don't mark up content that is not visible to readers of the page'; 'Your structured data must be a true representation of the page content'; 'Don't mark up irrelevant or misleading content, such as fake reviews'. The visible byline is 'the Harbor Line Team', and the owner's notes confirm the reviewer never read the page and the ratings were copied from Google Business Profile.

assertions.text: Does not claim that E-E-A-T is itself a direct or specific ranking factor; if E-E-A-T is discussed, it's consistent with Google's statement that it isn't a specific ranking factor, while Google's systems give even more weight to content aligned with strong E-E-A-T on YMYL topics like health.
assertions.rationale: Google: 'While E-E-A-T itself isn't a specific ranking factor...'; for topics that could significantly impact health, financial stability, or safety, 'our systems give even more weight to content that aligns with strong E-E-A-T'.

assertions.text: Recommends showing genuine, verifiable expertise the clinic actually has (e.g., the licensed DPTs/OCS as named authors or reviewers with credentials and a real review date) rather than borrowed or fabricated credentials.
assertions.rationale: Real, visible authorship by qualified clinicians is honest and is the kind of trust evidence readers and quality systems can verify.

assertions.text: Sets realistic expectations rather than promising citations, e.g., that hospitals and national health bodies are likely to keep being cited for general medical questions, that no change guarantees an AI citation, and/or that local or service-intent queries are a more achievable target.
assertions.rationale: Overpromising citations against hospitals and the NHS on broad medical queries would mislead the owner about what's achievable.

evals.topic: Scaling an AI-generated content program on a YMYL (personal finance) site
evals.prompt: I'm head of growth at Penny & Pine, a personal-finance publisher (~400 articles, all written by staff). The plan for Q4: use an LLM pipeline to generate 6,000 pages titled 'Cost of living in {city}: is it affordable on {salary}?' for every US city over 20k people, by filling a template with public census and rent data. Each page will carry the byline 'Reviewed by Jordan Hale, CFP'. Jordan is a persona we'd create, with a stock photo. The goal is to get these pages cited in AI Overviews and ChatGPT answers. My CEO wants to know: is this allowed by Google, and is it a good idea? Give me a straight answer and what you'd do instead or in addition.
evals.expected_output: Google doesn't prohibit AI-generated content as such ('Appropriate use of AI or automation is not against our guidelines'). Its guidance says generative AI can be useful, but content must meet Search Essentials and the spam policies. Generating many pages without adding value for users is named as an example of scaled content abuse, and that's true however the content is produced. 6,000 near-identical template pages with mostly public data are at real risk of falling into that. Personal finance is YMYL, where Google's systems give more weight to trust signals. Accuracy matters too: LLMs can produce wrong figures, and Google says to review AI content, including titles, descriptions, and structured data, for accuracy. The fake 'Jordan Hale, CFP' persona is the clearest no. Inventing an expert reviewer and credential is deceptive to readers. It risks being a deceptive endorsement under FTC principles and misuses the CFP certification mark. If discovered, it damages trust in the whole site. Google encourages accurate authorship information and transparency about how automation was used. Better plan: pilot a small set (e.g., the 50–100 largest metros). Add something genuinely useful that isn't elsewhere: your own calculation/methodology, combined data sources with citations, staff analysis, a transparent 'how we built this' note. Have real staff review accuracy. Only expand to cities where pages stay distinct and useful, and don't index thin pages. Measure both search performance and whether AI answers cite them, and expand or prune based on results.

assertions.text: States accurately that Google does not ban AI-generated content per se, but that generating many pages without adding value for users can violate its scaled content abuse spam policy regardless of how the content is made.
assertions.rationale: Google spam policies define scaled content abuse as many pages generated 'for the primary purpose of manipulating search rankings and not helping users', 'no matter how it's created', with the example 'Using generative AI tools or other similar tools to generate many pages without adding value for users'. Google's AI-content FAQ (Feb 2023): 'Appropriate use of AI or automation is not against our guidelines.'

assertions.text: Clearly advises against the invented 'Jordan Hale, CFP' persona/credential as deceptive, and recommends using real, accurately identified reviewers or not claiming a review at all. (Mentioning legal, endorsement, or CFP-mark risk is welcome but not required.)
assertions.rationale: A fabricated expert endorsement misleads readers on a YMYL topic. It conflicts with Google's encouragement of accurate authorship and with FTC endorsement principles, and exposes the brand if discovered.

assertions.text: Mentions that AI-generated content (including titles, descriptions, and structured data) should be reviewed for accuracy before publishing, and/or that disclosing how automation was used can help readers.
assertions.rationale: Google's gen-AI guidance: 'It is critical to manually factcheck and review all AI-generated content for accuracy and trustworthiness before publishing', including metadata such as titles, meta descriptions, structured data and alt text; and 'consider adding information on how your content was created'.

assertions.text: Notes that personal finance is a YMYL topic where trust and accuracy carry extra weight.
assertions.rationale: Google: for topics that could significantly affect health, financial stability, or safety, its systems give more weight to content aligned with strong E-E-A-T.

assertions.text: Recommends adding original value beyond templated public data (e.g., the publisher's own methodology, analysis, or expert input) and/or limiting scale to pages that are genuinely distinct and useful.
assertions.rationale: Unique information is what separates a useful programmatic page from scaled filler, and it gives AI engines a reason to cite this source over the underlying public data.

assertions.text: Does not endorse publishing all 6,000 pages at once: it either recommends a staged or limited rollout (e.g., pilot a subset, measure search and AI-answer outcomes, then expand or prune) or recommends a different format altogether (e.g., fewer, deeper pages or a single interactive tool).
assertions.rationale: Both a pilot and a non-programmatic alternative limit site-wide quality risk; the point is not to bet the site on an untested mass launch, not to prescribe one rollout method.

evals.topic: Site-wide CMS/framework migration and lost AI/search visibility
evals.prompt: Fern Hollow Gear (outdoor gear shop + blog, www.fernhollowgear.com) moved from an old PHP CMS to a new Next.js site on 28 September. Same domain, new URL structure. Since then our guides have vanished from Google, including AI Overviews where our tent-sizing guide used to be cited, and Perplexity seems to cite us less. Attached are our redirect map and some header checks. Our developer wants to file a Change of Address in Search Console to speed things up. What's wrong and what's the priority order?
evals.expected_output: Priority 1: the production pages send `x-robots-tag: noindex, nofollow` (probably carried over from staging). That alone tells Google to drop them from the index, and only indexed, snippet-eligible pages can appear in AI Overviews/AI Mode. Remove it site-wide now and confirm with URL Inspection. Robots.txt is fine. Priority 2: the redirect map. The two blog redirects that have a new equivalent use 302 (temporary); use permanent 301/308. tent-sizing-guide goes through a 3-hop chain (old → /blog/tent-sizing → /guides/tent-sizing → /guides/tent-sizing-guide); point every old URL straight at the final destination and stop renaming. Five old articles are redirected to the homepage, which Google may treat as soft 404s. Map each to the closest relevant page, restore/republish the content, or return 404/410 if it's truly gone. Priority 3: update internal links and sitemaps to the final URLs and keep redirects in place for at least a year (ideally longer). Change of Address is not applicable: it's for moving between domains/subdomains, not path changes on the same domain. Afterwards, monitor indexing/coverage and re-check the AI answers you care about. Recovery takes recrawling, and other engines that use their own or Bing's index recover on their own schedules.

assertions.text: Identifies from the header checks that live production pages return an `x-robots-tag: noindex` header and treats removing it as the top priority.
assertions.rationale: Derivable from response-headers.txt. A site-wide noindex is enough on its own to explain disappearing from Google, so it outranks every other fix.

assertions.text: Explains that noindexed pages are excluded from Google's index and therefore can't appear as links in AI Overviews/AI Mode, which require pages to be indexed and snippet-eligible.
assertions.rationale: Google: to be shown as a supporting link in AI features a page must be indexed and eligible to be shown with a snippet.

assertions.text: Recommends replacing the 302 redirects with permanent redirects (301 or 308) and collapsing the multi-hop chain so old URLs redirect directly to the final destination.
assertions.rationale: Google: 'we recommend that you use HTTP permanent redirects if possible, such as 301 and 308' and 'we advise redirecting to the final destination directly'. The CSV shows 302s and a 3-hop chain for the tent-sizing guide.

assertions.text: Flags that redirecting several unrelated old articles to the homepage is problematic (may be treated as soft 404s) and recommends mapping to relevant equivalents, restoring the content, or returning 404/410.
assertions.rationale: Google: 'Don't redirect many old URLs to one irrelevant single URL destination, such as the home page of the new site... might be treated as a soft 404 error.' The CSV shows five articles redirected to the home page.

assertions.text: Correctly says the Change of Address tool doesn't apply to a same-domain URL-structure change (it's for moving between domains or subdomains).
assertions.rationale: Google: Change of Address is needed only when moving from one domain or subdomain to another, not for moving paths within the same domain.

assertions.text: Recommends keeping the redirects in place long-term (at least about a year) and/or updating internal links and sitemaps to the final URLs.
assertions.rationale: Google: 'Keep the redirects for as long as possible, generally at least 1 year'; change internal links to the new URLs and update sitemaps with the new URLs.

evals.topic: Multilingual content generated by unreviewed machine translation
evals.prompt: I run marketing for Kanaal Cycling Tours, a small Dutch company running bike holidays in the Netherlands and Belgium. Last month our developer ran all 1,150 of our English blog posts through a machine translation API into German, French, Spanish, Italian, Polish, Danish, Swedish, Japanese and Korean, about 10,000 new pages, published automatically under /de/, /fr/ and so on. Nobody on the team speaks most of these languages. We did set up hreflang. The goal is for German and French travellers asking ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google's AI Mode about Dutch cycling holidays to see us. Is this going to work, and what should we do now?
evals.expected_output: Probably not as-is, and it carries real risk. Google's scaled content abuse policy covers many pages that give users little value however they're produced, and its examples mention automated transformations such as translating. Machine translation isn't banned as such, but 10,000 unreviewed MT pages across nine languages nobody can check fits that risk pattern. Hreflang only tells Google which language version to show. It doesn't make a page good, and it doesn't address quality. Research suggests a large share of low-resource-language web content is low-quality multi-way MT. Unreviewed MT also often gets tourism facts and tone wrong, and anything wrong (prices, dates, booking terms, safety) becomes what an AI might quote back. Recommended: pick the markets that matter (German, French, and maybe one more based on actual bookings), and choose the subset of pages that serve those travellers: tour pages, practical planning guides, FAQs. Have fluent speakers (staff, freelancers, or native-speaking guides) post-edit and localize them: currency, travel from Germany/France, local holidays, terms people actually search. Remove or noindex the rest, especially Japanese/Korean/etc. with no market and no reviewer. Keep one language per page; Google detects language from visible content, not the lang attribute or URL. Don't auto-redirect by assumed language or adapt content by IP. Then build presence in those markets (local travel press, German/French cycling forums and guides) and track whether AI answers in those languages mention you.

assertions.text: Explains that ~10,000 unreviewed machine-translated pages risk being treated by Google as scaled, low-value content (its scaled content abuse policy covers many pages giving little value to users however they're produced, and its examples mention automated transformations such as translating); does not claim machine translation is banned as such.
assertions.rationale: Google's scaled content abuse definition applies 'no matter how it's created'; one example is scraping content to generate many pages 'including through automated transformations like synonymizing, translating' where little value is provided. That example is about scraped content, so the policy describes a risk for mass self-translation rather than an outright prohibition.

assertions.text: Does not suggest that hreflang fixes, or signals, content quality; if hreflang is mentioned, it's described as a way of indicating language/regional alternates.
assertions.rationale: The user may assume hreflang 'handles' international SEO. Correcting that misconception is central to the advice.

assertions.text: Recommends focusing review/post-editing by fluent speakers on the markets and pages that matter (e.g., German and French, high-value pages) and dealing with the unreviewed remainder (e.g., removing, noindexing, or unpublishing it until reviewed).
assertions.rationale: This focuses limited resources where travellers actually are and removes low-value scaled pages that could hurt the site.

assertions.text: Notes that unreviewed translations risk factual or practical errors (e.g., prices, dates, booking terms) that AI answers could repeat, and/or recommends localization beyond literal translation.
assertions.rationale: AI engines quote pages. Mistranslated facts become misinformation attributed to the brand, and travellers need locally relevant details.

assertions.text: If it discusses technical language handling, what it says is accurate (e.g., Google determines page language from visible content, not the lang attribute or URL; Google advises against automatically redirecting users by assumed language and against IP-based content adaptation).
assertions.rationale: Google: 'We don't use any code-level language information such as lang attributes, or the URL'; 'Avoid automatically redirecting' between language versions; 'Don't use IP analysis to adapt your content.'

assertions.text: If it cites research on machine-translated web content, it represents it accurately (e.g., Thompson et al., ACL Findings 2024, found much multi-way parallel web content is low-quality MT, especially in lower-resource languages), without overstating it as a search-ranking finding.
assertions.rationale: The paper is about the prevalence and quality of MT web content and its implications for LLM training data, not about ranking or citation effects.

evals.topic: Quick question: does a noarchive meta tag affect Microsoft Copilot?
evals.prompt: Quick one. Years ago our IT team added <meta name="robots" content="noarchive"> to every page of our law firm's site (Brightwater Legal, Toronto) to stop search engines showing cached copies. We rank fine on Bing but Microsoft Copilot never cites us. Could that tag be the reason? Yes or no and what to do. Keep it short.
evals.expected_output: Yes, very possibly. Microsoft has said that pages with NOARCHIVE aren't used in Copilot (formerly Bing Chat) answers or linked from them, though they still appear in normal Bing results. Bing's 2026 guidelines rewrite reportedly keeps this for Copilot and grounding. NOCACHE is the middle option: Copilot may use only the URL, title, and snippet. If you want to be cited, remove noarchive (Google no longer uses it anyway since cached pages went away), then re-check Copilot after Bing recrawls. Use Bing Webmaster Tools URL inspection/IndexNow to speed that up if you like. Removing it makes you eligible, but it doesn't guarantee citations.

assertions.text: Answers yes (or 'likely yes'): Microsoft has documented that NOARCHIVE content is not included in or linked from Bing Chat (now Copilot) answers, while still appearing in regular Bing search results.
assertions.rationale: Bing (Sept 2023): content tagged NOARCHIVE 'will not be included in Bing Chat answers, not be linked to in the answers' but will still appear in search results; Search Engine Journal (Feb 2026) reports the rewritten Bing Webmaster Guidelines keep this for Copilot and grounding.

assertions.text: Recommends removing the noarchive directive if they want to be eligible for Copilot citations (and does not recommend NOCACHE as a way to get full citations).
assertions.rationale: Removing the tag is the direct fix. NOCACHE limits Copilot to URL, title, and snippet; per Search Engine Journal (Feb 2026), Bing's guidelines recommend against NOCACHE on content intended for Copilot if you want richer citations.

assertions.text: Does not claim that removing the tag guarantees Copilot citations.
assertions.rationale: The tag controls eligibility. Being chosen as a source still depends on relevance and quality.

assertions.text: Is brief, as requested: a direct yes/no-style answer with a short action, not a full audit.
assertions.rationale: The user explicitly asked for a short answer to a narrow question.

assertions.text: If Google is mentioned, does not claim noarchive affects Google's AI Overviews/AI Mode; Google says it no longer uses noarchive.
assertions.rationale: Google's robots meta tag docs say noarchive is no longer used by Google Search since the cached link feature no longer exists.

evals.topic: B2B original research report launch and PR campaign
evals.prompt: I'm the content lead at Tallyroll (payroll software for mid-market companies). We're launching our first big original research report in three weeks. Our goal is that when people ask AI assistants things like 'how common are payroll errors' or 'how much does a payroll error cost', the answers cite our numbers and mention us. Attached: the landing page draft and our launch plan. Please review it and tell me what to change.
evals.expected_output: As drafted, nothing crawlable states the findings. The headline stats are only in an image (alt text 'report stats'). The PDF sits behind a form and is served from a path robots.txt disallows, so crawlers and AI fetchers can't read your numbers or attribute them to you. Publish an ungated HTML summary page with the key findings as text: each stat as a clear, self-contained sentence with its population and date (e.g., '41% of US mid-market companies surveyed ran at least one off-cycle payroll to fix an error in 2025'). Include the methodology (n=1,140 US payroll leaders, fielded May–June 2026, panel sample weighted by company size), named authors, and a stable URL. Keep the gate for the full PDF or extra assets if you need leads, and make the PDF crawlable if it should be cited. Publish the aggregated tables legal approved (as HTML/CSV). Dataset markup is optional and aimed at Dataset Search; it requires name and description. Fix the PR plan. Wire releases with keyword anchor text like 'best payroll software' are named link spam by Google; use plain branded/report links (or nofollow) that point at the findings page. Paying listicle sites to cite you and rank you #1 is an undisclosed paid placement that misleads readers; disclose or drop it. Spend instead on journalists, analysts, and communities who'll cite the data on its merits. Research on generative engines (e.g., the GEO paper) suggests that adding statistics, quotations, and citations can raise visibility in tested setups, but results vary by domain and engine, so treat it as promising evidence, not a guarantee. Track whether AI answers to your target questions cite the report after launch.

assertions.text: Identifies from the fixtures that the key findings aren't available as crawlable text: they appear only in an image with uninformative alt text, and the full report is gated behind a form and/or on a robots.txt-disallowed path.
assertions.rationale: Derivable from report-landing.html. Engines can only cite and attribute numbers they can retrieve as text.

assertions.text: Recommends an ungated, indexable page (the landing page itself or a separate one) presenting the key statistics as text, with methodology details (e.g., sample size, population, fieldwork dates, weighting) so the numbers are attributable and verifiable. Keeping the full PDF gated is compatible with this.
assertions.rationale: Self-contained, sourced statistics with methodology are what journalists and AI answers can quote accurately.

assertions.text: Flags that press releases distributed with keyword-rich anchor-text links (e.g., 'best payroll software') fall under Google's link spam policy, and recommends removing them or using plain/branded or qualified (nofollow/sponsored) links.
assertions.rationale: Google's link spam examples include 'links with optimized anchor text in articles, guest posts, or press releases distributed on other sites.'

assertions.text: Flags the plan to pay listicle sites to cite the report and rank Tallyroll #1 as problematic (e.g., a paid placement that misleads readers unless clearly disclosed, and/or a paid link scheme), and recommends dropping it or clearly disclosing the payment (and qualifying any paid links).
assertions.rationale: Undisclosed paid endorsements mislead readers and conflict with FTC endorsement disclosure principles; Google's link spam policy lists 'Exchanging money for links, or posts that contain links'.

assertions.text: If Dataset structured data is recommended, it is described accurately (aimed at dataset discovery, e.g., Dataset Search, with name and description required) and not as a requirement for AI citation.
assertions.rationale: Google's Dataset docs: the markup's purpose is to improve discovery of datasets; required properties are name and description.

assertions.text: If it cites research that adding statistics/citations increases generative-engine visibility, it presents it with appropriate caveats (e.g., experimental results that vary by domain/engine) rather than as a guaranteed effect.
assertions.rationale: Aggarwal et al. (KDD 2024) report visibility gains of up to 40% in their benchmark, and note efficacy varies across domains.

evals.topic: Marketplace with user reviews: review practices, review markup, and AI reputation
evals.prompt: I'm co-founder of TradeNest, a US marketplace connecting homeowners with local plumbers and electricians. When people ask ChatGPT or Perplexity 'is TradeNest legit' or 'best site to find a plumber', we're either missing or described as 'mixed reviews'. Our growth plan: (1) use an LLM to turn tradespeople's job notes into ~2,000 customer reviews to seed new city pages, (2) give customers a $10 credit when they leave a 5-star review, (3) automatically hide reviews under 3 stars 'for quality', and (4) add AggregateRating schema for TradeNest itself to our homepage so we get stars in Google. Thoughts?
evals.expected_output: Stop items 1–3. They're illegal in the US, not just risky. The FTC's Consumer Reviews and Testimonials Rule (16 CFR Part 465, in effect since October 2024) prohibits reviews that misrepresent that they come from real customers with real experience, including AI-generated ones. It prohibits incentives conditioned on a particular sentiment (a $10 credit for 5 stars), and suppressing reviews by rating while implying the displayed reviews represent all or most of what was submitted (sentiment-neutral filtering for fake, abusive, or unrelated content is allowed). The FTC can seek civil penalties per violation and sent warning letters in December 2025. Item 4: Google treats reviews a business controls about itself as self-serving, so Organization/LocalBusiness review stars on your own site aren't eligible. Fake reviews also violate Google's structured data policies. Do instead: ask every customer for a review after a verified job, with any incentive offered regardless of rating. Show all reviews with neutral moderation rules published, respond to negative ones, and fix the root causes behind them. Earn presence on independent platforms (independent review sites, local community forums, press). Publish transparent trust info (how you vet pros, guarantees, complaint handling). AI answers summarize what independent sources say, so a 'mixed reviews' description changes only when the underlying experience and third-party sentiment change. Track it over time.

assertions.text: States that AI-generated or otherwise fabricated customer reviews (reviews misrepresenting that they're from real customers with actual experience) are prohibited under the FTC's consumer reviews rule.
assertions.rationale: The FTC rule bans reviews that misrepresent they are by someone who doesn't exist, such as AI-generated fake reviews, or by someone without actual experience.

assertions.text: States that offering an incentive conditioned on a positive (e.g., 5-star) review is prohibited, while noting or allowing that incentives offered regardless of sentiment are a different matter.
assertions.rationale: 16 CFR 465.4 bans compensation conditioned on reviews expressing a particular sentiment, positive or negative.

assertions.text: Flags that hiding reviews based on low ratings while presenting the displayed reviews as representative is prohibited review suppression; neutral, consistently applied moderation (e.g., removing fake, abusive, or unrelated reviews) is permissible.
assertions.rationale: 16 CFR 465.7(b) prohibits misrepresenting displayed reviews as representing most or all reviews when they're suppressed based on rating or negative sentiment, with exceptions for criteria applied equally regardless of sentiment.

assertions.text: Explains that review/rating markup about TradeNest placed on TradeNest's own site is self-serving and not eligible for Google review stars.
assertions.rationale: Google: if the entity being reviewed controls the reviews about itself, its LocalBusiness/Organization pages are ineligible for the star review feature.

assertions.text: Recommends legitimate alternatives: soliciting reviews from all verified customers without sentiment conditions, showing negative reviews and responding to them, and/or addressing the service issues behind them.
assertions.rationale: Honest review collection builds the independent sentiment AI answers summarize, without legal exposure.

assertions.text: Notes that AI descriptions of a brand's reputation draw heavily on independent third-party sources, so improving the real customer experience and/or earning genuine coverage on independent platforms matters more than on-site manipulation.
assertions.rationale: 'Is X legit' answers synthesize external reviews and discussions the brand doesn't control, so on-site changes alone won't change them.
